alt: Anatomy of a body paragraph using the home-gardens example: a topic sentence stating the main idea, development with an explanation and an example, and a linking sentence (However, gardens also bring problems) that prepares the next paragraph.
caption: Figure: the parts of a body paragraph (topic sentence, development, linking sentence)

alt: Routine for every composition: analyse the title, plan five or six paragraphs, write, then check; in a one-hour paper about 5 minutes go on planning, 45 on writing and 10 on checking.
caption: Figure: analyse, plan, write, check, with a 5, 45 and 10 minute split for one hour

alt: Layout of a formal letter in order: writer's address and date at top right, recipient's title and address on the left, salutation, bold subject line, opening paragraph stating the purpose, detail paragraphs, a closing paragraph asking for action, then the close, signature and full name.
caption: Figure: the layout of a formal letter (schematic)

alt: Inference method applied to Nyasha reading her results: the clues (read the list twice, hid her face, stayed in the toilets) mean she was upset, so the inference is that her results were probably disappointing, supported by the evidence that she kept her face turned towards the wall.
caption: Figure: clue, meaning, inference, evidence for the Nyasha extract

alt: The GAP check applied to a report to the Head: genre is report, audience is the Head so the language is formal and respectful, and purpose is to inform and recommend.
caption: Figure: reading a task for Genre, Audience and Purpose (GAP)

alt: Register scale from formal to informal: formal for head, officials and editors with precise words and no contractions; semi-formal for club members; informal for friends with everyday words and contractions; slang and text speak are never acceptable in an exam.
caption: Figure: formal, semi-formal and informal register compared

alt: Layout of a report in order: title, To/From/Date, introduction or terms of reference, optional procedure, findings under sub-headings (facts only), conclusion, numbered recommendations and the signature with name and position.
caption: Figure: the eight parts of a report (schematic page)

alt: Process for selecting summary points: dissect the question for focus, whose or what and limits; read the whole passage once; underline only what answers the focus; keep one idea per point; then make numbered notes in your own words.
caption: Figure: the five steps for selecting summary points

alt: Process for writing up a summary: start directly with a point, use your own words, combine points into fluent sentences, link them logically in a paragraph, and check the word count and accuracy.
caption: Figure: the five steps for writing a summary

alt: Writer's craft method applied to the word swallowed in the flood sentence: identify the word, give its meaning in context (covered completely), explain its connotation (hungry, powerful, final) and state the effect on the reader (a greedy animal, danger felt).
caption: Figure: identify, meaning, connotation, effect for the word swallowed
